concepts.name: Decision, options and criteria
concepts.summary: Identify the decision to be made, the available options and the criteria that matter for judging them.

concepts.name: Risk versus uncertainty
concepts.summary: Explain that outcomes of a choice are not certain and distinguish known probabilities from unknown ones.

concepts.name: Pros and cons listing
concepts.summary: Use a simple pros and cons list to compare options and explain its limits when items differ in importance.

concepts.name: Reversible versus irreversible choices
concepts.summary: Tell apart decisions that can be undone cheaply from those that cannot and explain why this affects how much care to take.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
aliases: cost of the next best alternative
concepts.summary: Explain that choosing one option means giving up the value of the best alternative forgone.

concepts.name: Outcome versus decision quality
concepts.summary: Recognise that a good decision can have a bad outcome through luck and vice versa.

concepts.name: Common bias names
concepts.summary: Recall and describe in plain words anchoring, sunk cost and overconfidence as ways judgment goes wrong.

misconceptions.text: A good decision is one that turns out well.
Choosing to do nothing has no cost.
A pros and cons list with more pros than cons means that option should win.

concepts.name: Estimating probabilities
concepts.summary: Assign rough numeric probabilities to outcomes using base rates and available evidence.

concepts.name: Expected value calculation
concepts.summary: Compute the expected value of an option by multiplying each outcome's payoff by its probability and summing.

concepts.name: Drawing a decision tree
concepts.summary: Lay out decision nodes, chance nodes and payoffs in a tree for a simple choice.

concepts.name: Weighted decision matrix
concepts.summary: Score options against weighted criteria and total the results to compare them.

concepts.name: Basic cost-benefit comparison
concepts.summary: List and put money values on costs and benefits of an option and compare net benefit.

concepts.name: Sunk cost recognition
concepts.summary: Spot past unrecoverable costs in a situation and exclude them from the forward-looking choice.

concepts.name: Anchoring in estimates
concepts.summary: Notice how a first number shapes later estimates and apply simple countermeasures such as forming an estimate before seeing others.

misconceptions.text: The option with the highest expected value is always the right choice.
Weights and scores in a decision matrix are objective facts rather than judgments.
Money already spent should count in deciding whether to continue.

concepts.name: Utility and risk attitude
concepts.summary: Analyse why expected utility can differ from expected value and how diminishing marginal utility explains risk aversion.

concepts.name: Multi-stage decision trees
concepts.summary: Solve trees with sequential decisions by folding back from the final payoffs to the first choice.

concepts.name: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.summary: Vary probabilities, weights and payoffs to find which inputs change the preferred option.

concepts.name: Regret and minimax analysis
concepts.summary: Build a regret table and compare it with maximin and maximax when probabilities are unknown.

concepts.name: Discounting and time value
concepts.summary: Adjust costs and benefits occurring at different times to present value in cost-benefit analysis.

concepts.name: Pre-mortem technique
concepts.summary: Run a pre-mortem by assuming the plan failed and listing the likely causes to find weaknesses before committing.

concepts.name: Calibration and overconfidence
concepts.summary: Analyse the gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy and use interval estimates and track records to correct it.

concepts.name: Value of information
concepts.summary: Judge whether gathering more information is worth its cost by estimating how much it could change the decision.

misconceptions.text: Risk aversion is irrational because it departs from maximising expected value.
A sensitivity analysis is only needed if you doubt your best estimates.
Feeling very sure about an estimate means it is likely to be accurate.

concepts.name: Framing and prospect theory
concepts.summary: Analyse how gain versus loss framing, reference points and loss aversion shift choices away from expected utility.

concepts.name: Decision under deep uncertainty
concepts.summary: Choose between approaches such as robustness, scenario planning and option preservation when probabilities cannot be credibly assigned.

concepts.name: Real options and reversibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate the value of keeping options open, staging commitments and delaying irreversible choices.

concepts.name: Bayesian updating of beliefs
concepts.summary: Revise probability estimates in a decision model as new evidence arrives, respecting base rates.

concepts.name: Multi-criteria trade-offs
concepts.summary: Critique and select methods for combining conflicting criteria, including rank reversal and weight-elicitation problems.

concepts.name: Group decision pitfalls
concepts.summary: Analyse how groupthink, authority and shared-information bias degrade group decisions and how structured methods counter them.

concepts.name: Decision process evaluation
concepts.summary: Assess decision quality separately from outcomes using records of reasoning, assumptions and forecasts.

misconceptions.text: Biases can be removed by simply knowing about them.
When probabilities are unknown, any numeric estimate is as good as none and analysis is pointless.
Delaying a decision to keep options open is always the safer choice.

concepts.name: Choosing decision methods
concepts.summary: Judge which technique fits a given decision's stakes, uncertainty, time and data, including when to use heuristics instead of formal analysis.

concepts.name: Heuristics and ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Evaluate when simple rules outperform complex models and when they systematically mislead.

concepts.name: Noise and judgment variability
concepts.summary: Distinguish noise from bias in repeated judgments and apply practices such as independent assessment and structured scoring to reduce it.

concepts.name: Designing decision architecture
concepts.summary: Design organisational procedures, defaults, checklists and review gates that reduce bias and noise in recurring decisions.

concepts.name: Modelling strategic interaction
concepts.summary: Assess decisions where others respond to your choice by incorporating their incentives and likely reactions.

concepts.name: Tail risk and ruin avoidance
concepts.summary: Evaluate choices where rare catastrophic losses make expected-value reasoning misleading and impose survival constraints.

concepts.name: Building a decision framework
concepts.summary: Create a tailored end-to-end framework combining framing, modelling, pre-mortem, review and learning loops for a domain.

misconceptions.text: More elaborate quantitative models always yield better decisions than simple rules.
Inconsistency between different people's judgments is just diversity of views, not a flaw.
Maximising expected value is safe for any repeated gamble regardless of possible ruin.
